title: Constipation Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing constipation, recognising serious causes and complications, distinguishing functional constipation from organic pathology, and supporting safe management and safety-netting.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, urgent investigation or escalation when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Acute bowel obstruction (absolute constipation, abdominal distension, vomiting, lack of flatus).
Faecal impaction (hard stool palpable on rectal examination, overflow diarrhoea, urinary retention).
Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) after surgery or severe illness.
Colorectal cancer or polyp (change in bowel habit, blood in stool, weight loss, age >50).
Inflammatory bowel disease or stricture.
Acute abdomen or perforation risk.
Neurological cause (spinal cord compression, Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis).
Medication-related (opioids, anticholinergics, iron supplements).
items.importantLimitation: Constipation can mask serious pathology. Red-flag features warrant investigation even in apparently low-risk patients.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Characterise constipation onset, severity and associated symptoms to guide diagnosis.

items.title: Constipation characteristics
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: acute vs. chronic (gradual change vs. long-standing); duration and progression.
Frequency: days since last bowel movement; previously normal frequency.
Stool: hard, pellet-like, normal consistency but infrequent?
Effort: straining, difficulty passing stool, feeling of incomplete emptying.
Associated: abdominal bloating, distension, cramping or pain.

items.title: Change in bowel habit
mustConfirmOrExclude: Acute change from patient's usual pattern.
Narrowing of stool (pencil-thin stools suggest stricture or mass).
Alternate constipation and diarrhoea.
Blood in stool or rectal bleeding.
Mucus in stool.

items.title: Red-flag features in history
mustConfirmOrExclude: Absolute constipation (no stool or flatus for several days).
Abdominal pain, distension or vomiting.
Involuntary weight loss or loss of appetite.
Blood in stool or visible rectal bleeding.
Age >50 with new-onset constipation.
Family history of colorectal cancer.
Recent opioid use or medication change.
Recent surgery, spinal injury or neurological disease.
Urinary retention or neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness).

items.title: Risk factors for constipation
mustConfirmOrExclude: Medications: opioids, anticholinergics (antihistamines, antispasmodics), iron supplements, diuretics.
Low dietary fibre or inadequate fluid intake.
Immobility or sedentary lifestyle.
Neurological disease (Parkinson's, spinal cord disease, stroke).
Endocrine disease (hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, diabetes).
Recent surgery or hospitalisation.

sections.title: Serious pathology screen
sections.intro: Positive features should trigger urgent investigation or referral.

items.title: Acute bowel obstruction
urgentFeatures: Absolute constipation (no stool or flatus for >12 hours).
Abdominal distension and pain.
Vomiting or bilious vomiting.
Abdominal tenderness or peritoneal signs.
implications: Emergency hospital assessment; abdominal imaging (CT or AXR) required.

items.title: Faecal impaction
urgentFeatures: Hard stool palpable on rectal examination.
Overflow diarrhoea or liquid stool around impacted mass.
Urinary retention or incontinence.
Confusion or delirium (in elderly; may be sole presenting symptom).
Often following immobility, opioid use or inadequate fibre.
implications: Manual disimpaction (if necessary), stool softeners, enemas; hospital admission may be needed.

items.title: Colorectal cancer
urgentFeatures: Age >50 with new-onset constipation.
Pencil-thin stools or change in stool calibre.
Blood in stool or visible rectal bleeding.
Involuntary weight loss.
Abdominal mass or tenesmus.
implications: Urgent referral for colonoscopy or CT colonography.

items.title: Colonic perforation or pseudo-obstruction
urgentFeatures: Acute abdominal pain with distension.
Fever and signs of peritonitis.
Often after surgery, severe illness or opioid use.
Risk of toxic megacolon (see acute diarrhoea).
implications: Emergency hospital assessment; abdominal imaging and possible surgery.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Examine for complications, signs of serious pathology and stool impaction.

items.title: Abdominal examination
howToTest: Inspect: distension, visible peristalsis, scars from prior surgery.
Palpate: tenderness (diffuse vs. localised), masses, guarding or rebound.
Auscultate: bowel sounds (present, reduced, absent, high-pitched).
normal: Soft, non-tender, normal bowel sounds, no distension.
abnormal: Distension, tenderness, peritoneal signs, absent bowel sounds, palpable mass.
implications: Distension + absent bowel sounds suggests obstruction; peritoneal signs suggest perforation.

items.title: Digital rectal examination
howToTest: Inspect perianal area: fissures, haemorrhoids, fistulae, tags.
Palpate rectum: hard stool (impaction), masses, stricture, tenderness.
Assess anal sphincter tone and sensation.
normal: Patent rectum, normal tone, no masses, no blood.
abnormal: Hard stool impaction, palpable mass, stricture, blood, reduced sensation.
implications: Impacted stool confirms impaction; palpable mass raises cancer concern; blood warrants investigation.

items.title: Neuromuscular assessment
howToTest: Lower-limb strength and sensation (spinal cord compression risk).
Reflexes and perianal sensation (spinal cord syndrome).
Signs of Parkinson's or other neurological disease.
normal: Normal strength, sensation, reflexes and gait.
abnormal: Weakness, sensory loss, hyperreflexia or absent reflexes, gait disturbance.
implications: Neurological signs suggest spinal cord compression or neurological disease requiring urgent investigation.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Pattern recognition supports diagnosis and management decisions.

items.title: Functional constipation
commonFindings: Associated with low fibre, low fluid intake or sedentary lifestyle.
Responds to dietary modification and laxatives.
implications: Dietary advice, fluid intake, exercise, stool softeners; laxatives as needed.

items.title: Opioid-induced constipation
commonFindings: Follows opioid initiation or dose increase.
Often severe and may not respond to simple measures.
Occurs even with adequate fibre and fluid.
implications: Proactive laxative regimen required (stool softener + stimulant); consider opioid reduction if possible.

items.title: Medication-related constipation (other)
commonFindings: Follows anticholinergic drug (antihistamine, antispasmodic), iron supplement or diuretic.
Improves with drug withdrawal or dose reduction.
implications: Review medications; consider alternatives if possible; temporary laxative support.

items.title: Faecal impaction (elderly/immobile)
commonFindings: Often follows immobility, opioid use, dehydration or inadequate fibre.
May present with overflow diarrhoea, urinary retention or confusion.
implications: Manual disimpaction (with analgesia/sedation if needed); laxatives and prevention strategy.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Base decisions on serious pathology assessment, severity and complications.

items.title: Investigation
mustConfirmOrExclude: Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy: if age >50 or new-onset constipation or alarm features.
Abdominal imaging (X-ray or CT): if acute obstruction suspected.
Blood tests: if weight loss, anaemia suspected or systemic disease (TSH, calcium, glucose).
Digital rectal examination: always performed to assess for impaction and masses.

items.title: Community management is appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No red-flag features present.
No absolute constipation or signs of obstruction.
No palpable mass on rectal examination.
Likely functional constipation or medication-related.
Patient able to manage with lifestyle modification and laxatives.

items.title: Urgent investigation or referral
urgentFeatures: Absolute constipation with abdominal pain and distension (obstruction).
Red-flag features: age >50 with new constipation, blood in stool, weight loss.
Palpable abdominal mass or rectal mass.
Signs of spinal cord compression (weakness, sensory loss).
Faecal impaction requiring manual disimpaction.
implications: Urgent colonoscopy or imaging; hospital assessment if acute obstruction suspected.

items.title: Constipation
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: severe abdominal pain with distension and vomiting (obstruction); abdominal pain with inability to pass stool or flatus; signs of peritonitis (severe tenderness); or signs of spinal cord compression (weakness or numbness in legs).

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: no bowel movement for more than 3 days with abdominal discomfort; blood in stool; involuntary weight loss; change in stool calibre; or severe straining causing pain or bleeding.
Speak to your GP if: constipation persists despite laxatives; you are having to use increasingly strong laxatives; or you want advice about medication-related constipation.
